about: Latest official NWS weather for La Porte, IN, saved hourly for laporteweathernow.com's homepage (scripts/home_cache.py).

daily.name: Tonight
daily.shortForecast: Mostly Cloudy then Light Rain Likely

sections.title: KEY MESSAGES
paragraphs: - Another round of rain late tonight into Sunday night followed by blustery/windy conditions behind a cold front Sunday night. Rainfall amounts between one quarter and three quarters of an inch are expected.

- The coldest conditions are expected Monday and Monday night followed by a warming trend to much above normal temperatures by Thursday and Friday. The next chance of rain will be late in the upcoming work week.

sections.title: DISCUSSION
paragraphs: Short wave upper ridging has shifted eastward across the southern Great Lakes and Ohio River valley this morning providing a brief period of clear skies early this morning. Looking upstream, a lee trough feature is progressing eastward and is gaining at least some amplitude across the Corn Belt as a 100 knot jet streak shifts through the base of this trough. The mid level trough axis appears to mark a fairly strong gradient in elevated 900-800 mb moisture and this forcing and accompanying moisture axis will shift into the local area after 12Z this morning. The limiting factor for precipitation continues to be the lack of better near sfc moisture and maintenance of a relatively dry subcloud layer. There have been some reports of light rain upstream across eastern Iowa, but in association with cigs of 5-6k feet. Did include a mention of chance sprinkles (possibly few flurries) following the eastward progression of this forcing this morning. By this afternoon, clouds should decrease from west to east behind this short wave, with low level warm advection becoming a bit more pronounced in its wake. Higher res guidance does suggest development of modest boundary layer this afternoon with a few afternoon southwest gusts to 20 mph possible.

For tonight, the Mid MS Valley/southern Great Lakes should become situated more into a col region as a more vigorous short wave trough digs southeast across the Rockies and into the southern Plains. This will result in a broad sector of strengthening southwest flow from the southern plains into eastern Missouri by late evening with the nose of this stronger flow beginning to impinge on central Indiana toward daybreak Sunday. This evolution will allow for rapid northward low level moisture transport from the Gulf, and weak speed convergence at nose of this stronger low level flow will likely support a wing of advective rain overnight into early Sunday morning. These leading advective wing precip bands are sometimes difficult to pinpoint given they occur well east of the stronger dynamic synoptic forcing, so additional refinements in PoPs will be needed when confidence in location/timing can be resolved.

Rain chances should ramp up quickly area-wide during the day Sunday as digging nature of upper trough and strong moisture transport continue, and low/mid level baroclinic zone rapidly strengthens. This strengthening baroclinicity should also enhance upper jet streak magnitude with some additional synoptic contribution in left exit region of an Ohio Valley upper jet streak. Given PWAT's of close to an inch across NE IN/NW Ohio, storm total rainfall amounts in the southeast could reach the half inch to three quarters of an inch rain, but progressive nature of best moisture axis should prevent any notable hydro issues. Can't completely rule out an isolated rumble of thunder far southeast with some very weak elevated instability possible, but better thunder potential still appears to be across southern Indiana for Sunday.

Passage of sfc reflection to the south and the associated strong baroclinic zone will mark onset of some stronger northwest winds by late Sunday afternoon and more likely by Sunday evening/overnight. Strongest isallobaric forcing push may end up remaining south of local area where RAP suggests 3-hr pressure rises on the order of 8-10 mb. This could promote a brief period of 40+ mph wind gusts across portions of central and possibly into northeast Indiana at least for a brief time later Sunday evening. Of greater confidence is wind gusts into the 25 to 35 mph range for at least a time Sunday night. Some weak lake response is possible late Sunday night in the form of a few snow showers, but instability depths in this particular setup appear quite shallow.

Winds should drop of noticeably by daybreak Monday as elongated north-south oriented low level ridge axis shifts into the region. Monday still appears to be coldest day of this period with highs likely not getting out of the upper 30s behind this system as low level thermal trough anchors across eastern Great Lakes and low level thermal advection becomes neutral locally.

Confidence remains high in a warming trend for the remainder of the week as split-type flow develops across western CONUS with broad negative southern stream height anomaly shifting to the southern Plains by late Thursday. GFS deterministic remains somewhat of a slow outlier in eastward progression of this feature with more separation and delayed phasing with northern stream in comparison to Canadian/EC. GFS ensemble means do tend to provide a little more support to the EC/Canadian camp however. Current trend in blended PoPs supports idea of a compromise of these two camps with more weight to the non-deterministic GFS consensus in higher rain chance PoPs ramping up by late Thursday night. High temperatures by Thursday and Friday will be much above normal into the 50s and possibly even some lower 60s in some areas by Friday depending on precip evolution.
